demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette: David is a 34-year-old North American male, married, and works as a school counselor. He has been struggling with symptoms of PTSD following an incident at work where he accidentally caused serious injury to another person. The trauma of the event and its aftermath have profoundly impacted his daily life. The traumatic event occurred during a routine day at the school when David was trying to break up a heated argument between two students. In his attempt to diffuse the situation, he inadvertently pushed one student too hard, resulting in a severe injury that required immediate medical attention. The memory of this incident remains vivid and distressing for him. David experiences intense triggers related to stress, undergoing medical procedures, and certain smells reminiscent of the day of the accident. These triggers have significantly influenced his behavior and thought processes over time. When he encounters these stimuli, David often finds himself unable to think clearly or focus on anything else but the traumatic event. This has led him to adopt several maladaptive strategies such as keeping his mind occupied all the time and avoiding any situations that might remind him of police involvement. His constant vigilance is not just about staying busy; it is also tied to an intense fear of reliving the trauma or being faced with similar situations again. He is certain that his life has been irrevocably altered by this event, a belief that fuels his self-blame and doubt in his ability to act correctly in future scenarios. David's memories of the incident are particularly distressing as they feel entirely present and real each time they come back to him. The full sensory reliving of the moment makes it seem like he is still in the midst of the trauma, which exacerbates his negative emotions such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. These intense feelings are often triggered by related smells or stressful situations at work, further reinforcing his negative appraisals about himself and his life. His inability to trust that he can handle similar situations correctly has led him to avoid thinking about the event altogether. However, this avoidance only makes the memories more vivid when they do surface. The distressing nature of these recollections often causes strong physical reactions, such as increased heart rate and sweating, whenever something reminds him of the traumatic experience. David's sense that his life has been destroyed by the trauma is not just a fleeting thought but a deeply held belief that permeates his daily existence. This negative appraisal leads him to believe he cannot trust himself in critical moments, which drives his avoidance behaviors. For example, he avoids going to medical facilities for routine check-ups and finds it difficult to engage with students who remind him of the injured child. These maladaptive strategies have concrete consequences in David's life. As a school counselor, he often finds himself distracted or unable to concentrate on important tasks due to intrusive thoughts about the incident. This has affected his professional performance and relationships with colleagues, making him feel increasingly isolated at work. David's sleep is severely disrupted as he struggles to fall asleep, fearing that if he relaxes, he might relive the trauma in a dream. The constant state of alertness and the vivid recollections of the event make it difficult for him to function normally during the day. What finally brought David to seek help was an incident where he found himself unable to intervene effectively in another school conflict due to his overwhelming anxiety about repeating past mistakes. He is most afraid of never feeling safe again or being able to trust his judgment. However, he hopes that with support, he can regain a sense of control and move forward without the constant fear haunting him. David's current state reveals a self-reinforcing cycle where his triggers lead to maladaptive strategies, which in turn exacerbate his negative appraisals and memory disturbances, deepening his distress and vigilance. His journey towards recovery will require addressing these interwoven components of his trauma response.
